articles.title: Git worktrees using too much disk space? Copy-on-write can help
articles.description: I've been using coding agents a lot lately, usually with several tasks going on in parallel. Each...
articles.body_html:
I've been using coding agents a lot lately, usually with several tasks going on in parallel. Each gets a Git worktree so I can leave things open without switching branches all day. It works well. Except my disk kept filling up.

Every new worktree meant another checkout, and then there were the dependencies, generated files and build output. I started looking for a way to make those directories cheaper to keep around. I eventually wrote Parhel, a small Git extension in Rust that creates worktrees using copy-on-write (CoW).

Where the disk space goes

Git worktrees let you check out multiple branches of one repository into separate directories. I use them to keep a feature open while looking at something else, or to give different agents their own files to work on.

For example:

git worktree add -b feature/search ../my-app-search

Git already shares the repository's object database and most of its metadata. So a worktree isn't a full second Git clone. But Git checks out the working files again, and a fresh worktree doesn't bring along ignored directories such as:

  • node_modules/
  • .venv/
  • target/ in a Rust project
  • Compiled assets, generated code, and local caches

The usual next step is to install dependencies again or copy over the files you need. Do that across enough worktrees and the storage adds up. Package-manager caches help with part of it, but the generated output and other project files still need somewhere to live.

If you're curious about exactly what Git shares, its worktree documentation covers the layout.

How copy-on-write helps

Say you have a large node_modules/ directory and a few hundred megabytes of compiled output. You want another worktree, preferably with all of that ready to use.

Copying normally means writing all those bytes again. With CoW, the new files initially share data blocks with the originals. If you modify one of them, the filesystem allocates new blocks for what changed. You can edit the two copies independently; they just happen to share storage while their contents are the same.

There's some overhead for metadata, and the savings shrink as files diverge. But if you're mainly creating worktrees and editing source code while dependencies and build output stay largely unchanged, that's a useful tradeoff.

On Linux, the mechanism is commonly called a reflink. The FICLONE documentation describes how separate files can share storage until a write requires a copy.

You may not need anything beyond git worktree add. If your worktrees are small, there's little to gain. A shared package cache can also reduce how much a dependency installation costs. I wanted to reuse the working directory as a whole, including ignored files that aren't managed by a package manager.

Trying it with Parhel

Parhel is a Git external command, so after installing it you use git parhel. It creates an ordinary Git worktree from the directory you're working in, with CoW cloning wherever the filesystem allows it.

It brings the ignored directories too. You can still use git worktree list, move, lock and remove afterward. Nothing about the Git side of the workflow changes.

Install

On macOS with Homebrew:

brew install myrk-kale/tap/parhel

Or with Rust's package manager on macOS or Linux:

cargo install parhel

The Cargo installation requires Rust 1.85 or newer, and Parhel needs Git 2.29 or newer. There are also Linux .deb, .rpm, and release archives in the installation instructions.

Check that Git can find the command:

git parhel --version

Create a worktree

From your existing project:

git parhel add ../my-app-search --new-branch feature/search

Internally, Parhel registers a worktree with Git and clones the files from the source directory. The new worktree gets the dependencies and output that were already there, so in many projects you can just start working.

By default, Parhel expects a clean source worktree. If you intentionally want to carry over uncommitted changes and other untracked files, use --allow-dirty:

git parhel add ../my-app-experiment --new-branch experiment --allow-dirty

Changes that were staged in the source arrive unstaged in the new worktree.

Check your filesystem

On macOS, APFS already supports cloning. On Linux, Btrfs and XFS with reflink support can do it directly. ext4 needs a little more explanation.

System How Parhel uses CoW
macOS on APFS Native filesystem cloning via clonefile
Linux on Btrfs Reflink cloning
Linux on XFS with reflink enabled Reflink cloning
Linux on ext4 A one-time setup creates a separate Btrfs-backed CoW area

To check what Parhel can use on your machine:

git parhel doctor

On Linux, the doctor command can tell you when the directory's filesystem doesn't support reflinks. XFS needs to have reflinks enabled when the filesystem was created.

Ext4 needs a separate CoW area

ext4 doesn't support native reflinks. To make CoW work there, Parhel can create a Btrfs filesystem inside a sparse image and mount it as a separate area for your user. You set it up once:

sudo git parhel setup

This needs systemd, Btrfs support, and the tools listed in the Parhel documentation. It also makes system-level changes, so I recommend reading that part before running the command.

The first run copies the source into the Btrfs area as a baseline. That initial copy takes time and uses real space. Later worktrees share unchanged blocks with that baseline, and the path you asked for becomes a symlink to the worktree inside the store. ext4 itself hasn't gained CoW support; the sharing happens inside Btrfs.

You can also use --copy to make a full copy on any filesystem, or --fallback to use a regular Git worktree without copying the ignored files. Neither option saves disk space through CoW, but both work without setting up the store.

What I measured

I ran a benchmark on macOS with 78 MB of node_modules (about 20,000 files) and a 300 MB generated artifact. I compared getting a regular worktree ready by copying the ignored files over with creating one through Parhel.

Creating a ready-to-use worktree Time Additional disk space
git worktree add, followed by cp -R for dependencies and output 6.9 s 383 MiB
git parhel add 0.5 s About 8 MiB

The difference was pretty striking in that project. A plain git worktree add wouldn't copy the ignored directories in the first place, so the baseline includes cp -R to get both worktrees ready with the same files. You can find the details in the README; your results will depend on the files and filesystem involved.

A note about du

One thing that can be misleading: Finder and du -sh may report the full size of both directories after cloning. The files have their own logical sizes even when they're sharing blocks on disk.

I check how much free space changed before and after creating a worktree:

df -h .
# Create a worktree on the same filesystem.
df -h .

On ext4, remember to check the filesystem backing the store too. The initial baseline is a real copy, and the destination path points into the mounted Btrfs area.

Where you still need to be careful

.env files and external services

Parhel copies ignored files, which can include local credentials and .env files. If two worktrees contain the same database URL, they'll connect to the same database. A migration from one worktree can affect the other. That's worth thinking about before giving several agents their own working directories.

If a file needs different values per worktree, exclude it with .parhelignore and create a separate configuration in the destination:

.env
.env.*

.parhelignore uses Gitignore-style patterns and applies to untracked files Parhel would otherwise carry over. Git still controls tracked files.

Paths inside virtual environments

A Python virtual environment can contain scripts pointing to the directory where it was created. Symlinks and generated configuration from other tools can have the same problem.

Parhel rewrites source paths in untracked text files where it can and adjusts relevant symlinks. It leaves binary files alone because patching an embedded path could corrupt them. Some Conda environments, for example, are better left out through .parhelignore and rebuilt when needed.

The mechanism is generic. Parhel doesn't need to know whether a directory belongs to Python, Node.js, or another tool.

Removing a worktree

Git doesn't ask about ignored files when removing a worktree. If you had a local database or generated results in there, those can disappear along with it.

I recommend checking first:

git -C ../my-app-search status --ignored --short

For a normal CoW worktree, removal is the usual Git command:

git worktree remove ../my-app-search

Worktrees in the ext4-backed store are locked so Git won't forget them when the mount is unavailable. To remove one of those:

git worktree unlock ../my-app-search
git worktree remove ../my-app-search
git parhel doctor --fix

There are other edge cases, including sparse checkouts and submodules, covered in the README. I'd read those before using it on a repository you can't afford to disrupt.

I mostly use it with coding agents

The reason I started this was the number of parallel tasks I keep open with coding agents. I wanted to create another worktree and let an agent get on with its task without waiting for me to rebuild the environment.

Parhel works without an agent. If you use one, there's an optional skill in the repository that teaches it when to use Parhel and which details to check before copying or removing files:

npx skills add myrk-kale/parhel

You can install it globally with -g as well. The skill covers things like .env files and ignored content, which are easy to overlook when you're moving quickly.

I've kept Parhel focused on worktree creation. It doesn't replace the Git workflow I already have, and it should be just as useful if you don't use coding agents at all.

It's still a 0.x project. There are more than 430 tests covering Git operations and real filesystem behavior, but I'm sure there are setups I haven't seen yet. I've documented the tests, filesystem implementation, and known limitations in the repository.

If you've been dealing with the same disk space problem, I'd be interested to hear how you've handled it, especially if your worktrees have something Parhel won't copy safely.

articles.title: StartsWith Was Asking ICU Every Time
articles.description: The default StartsWith and IndexOf overloads compare text the culture-aware way, through ICU, not the literal char match you probably meant. I benchmarked the gap on two million lines and found IndexOf was the one quietly costing me.
articles.body_html:
I had an endpoint that sorts log lines as they come off a queue: route the ERROR ones one way, everything else another. The hot loop is one check, does this line start with "ERROR", and I'd written line.StartsWith("ERROR") without a second thought. It's the most obvious thing you can type.

Then I had the service under load with a profiler open, and a surprising slice of time was parked inside CompareInfo and the globalization stack underneath it. For a prefix check on ASCII log lines. That's when it clicked that StartsWith(string) doesn't do what I thought it did.

The default overload is linguistic, not literal

Here's the thing I'd forgotten. string.StartsWith(string) and string.IndexOf(string), the overloads that take only a string, don't compare characters. They compare text, using the current culture's rules, which on most boxes means routing through ICU for a full linguistic comparison. That's the machinery that knows "ﬀ" and "ff" are the same word, that a soft hyphen shouldn't count, that casing folds differently in Turkish. Handy when you're sorting names a person will read. Total overkill when you're asking whether a byte string begins with five known ASCII letters.

The fix is to say what you actually meant:

line.StartsWith("ERROR", StringComparison.Ordinal)

Ordinal means compare the char values, in order, and stop. No culture, no collation table, no ICU.

I counted it

I don't trust my gut on this stuff, so I wrote the smallest thing that would show the gap. Two million log-ish lines in an array, five prefixes mixed in so the comparison has to actually look at characters:

string[] prefixes = { "INFO ", "WARN ", "DEBUG ", "ERROR ", "TRACE " };
var lines = new string[2_000_000];
for (int i = 0; i < lines.Length; i++)
    lines[i] = prefixes[i % prefixes.Length] + "request " + i + " finished in " + (i % 400) + "ms";

Then count how many start with "ERROR", the polite way and the ordinal way:

static long CountCulture(string[] lines)
{
    long n = 0;
    foreach (string s in lines)
        if (s.StartsWith("ERROR")) n++;                       // CurrentCulture
    return n;
}

static long CountOrdinal(string[] lines)
{
    long n = 0;
    foreach (string s in lines)
        if (s.StartsWith("ERROR", StringComparison.Ordinal)) n++;
    return n;
}

The harness is nothing fancy. A stopwatch, a warmup call for each path so the JIT and the ICU tables are hot, then the best time out of seven, with the allocation counter read around each pass:

static long Measure(Action a, out long bestMs)
{
    bestMs = long.MaxValue;
    long bytes = 0;
    var sw = new Stopwatch();
    for (int run = 0; run < 7; run++)
    {
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        sw.Restart();
        a();
        sw.Stop();
        bytes = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before;
        if (sw.ElapsedMilliseconds < bestMs) bestMs = sw.ElapsedMilliseconds;
    }
    return bytes;
}

It's a single-file console app on .NET 10, top-level statements, nothing else in it. Here's what came back:

StartsWith (culture) :    27 ms
StartsWith (ordinal) :    18 ms
ratio                : 1.5x
allocated (culture)  : 0 bytes
allocated (ordinal)  : 0 bytes

That was a bit of a letdown, if I'm honest. I'd built this up in my head as the villain and it came in at 1.5x. Real, repeatable, but not the kind of number that changes your afternoon. And neither path allocates a byte, so this is pure CPU, no garbage to chase.

Then I ran the same question through IndexOf, because plenty of my "does this contain" checks are written the same lazy way:

IndexOf (culture)    :   109 ms
IndexOf (ordinal)    :    30 ms
ratio                : 3.6x

There's the one that was actually hurting. A substring search under a linguistic comparison is a lot more work than a prefix check. It can't just glance at the front, it has to weigh matches at every position with full collation rules. Roughly 3.6x on the same data. That's the call I should have been worried about from the start.

These are ratios off a Linux container, not a lab bench with the clocks pinned, so the absolute milliseconds will land somewhere else on your hardware. The shape holds up though: ordinal is cheaper, and substring search is cheaper by a lot more than a prefix check.

Ordinal isn't a free find-and-replace

Here's the caveat, and it's a real one. Ordinal and culture don't always give the same answer. That's the entire reason they're separate methods, and it's why you can't just sweep the codebase swapping one for the other.

string shy = "co­op.log";                       // a soft hyphen sits between "co" and "op"
shy.StartsWith("coop");                               // True  - culture treats the hyphen as invisible
shy.StartsWith("coop", StringComparison.Ordinal);     // False - ordinal sees the hidden char

Culture-aware comparison treats that soft hyphen as nothing, so it matches "coop". Ordinal sees nine characters and says no. For log routing, ordinal is exactly what I want: the literal content, invisible characters and all. For anything a human typed and expects to match "naturally", though, like search boxes, usernames, display sorting, the linguistic version is the correct one, and the extra cost is the price of being correct.

My rule of thumb now: if the strings are protocol rather than prose, so headers, enum names, file extensions, log levels, anything machine-generated, reach for Ordinal or OrdinalIgnoreCase by default. If a person wrote it and a person will read it, leave the culture-aware comparison where it is. The analyzer CA1310 flags exactly these call sites if you switch it on, which beats grepping for them by hand.

The quiet irony is that ordinal is both faster and usually what you meant for this kind of data. It's just not the default, and the default looks so harmless sitting there.

So what's the laziest string comparison hiding in your hot path? Check the Contains calls first, those are IndexOf underneath.

— still benchmarking corners of the standard library nobody asked me to

articles.title: How to Review AI-Generated Pull Requests: A Checklist Before You Merge
articles.description: A pull request can look perfect. Clean names, tidy functions, a green CI check. And half of the new...
articles.body_html:
A pull request can look perfect. Clean names, tidy functions, a green CI check. And half of the new tests can still assert nothing.

AI-written code does not look sloppy. It looks like a competent person wrote it, and that is exactly the problem. Your instincts for spotting bad code are tuned to messy code, and this is not messy.

If your team merges AI-generated code, here is a checklist to run before you do. Each item also notes what a bot can check for you, so your attention goes to the things only a human can judge.

1. Does it solve the actual problem?

AI is very good at satisfying the letter of a prompt while missing the intent. Before you read the diff, read the ticket. Write down in one sentence what this change should do.

Then look at the file list. If the ticket was about one endpoint and the pull request touches nine files, ask why. Agents love to "improve" things nobody asked them to touch.

Human's job: compare the change to the intent.
Bot's job: none. This one is yours.

2. Is the diff small enough to review?

If you cannot hold the change in your head, you cannot review it. A big AI-generated diff gets a skim and a quick approval, and that is where bugs get through.

If the diff is too large, send it back and ask for smaller pieces. This is not rude. It is the same thing you would ask of a human colleague.

Human's job: push back on size.
Bot's job: none. This one is yours.

3. Do the imports and APIs actually exist?

Generated code often calls methods or options that sound right but do not exist in your installed version. Confident-looking code is not proof.

For anything unfamiliar, check it against the official docs for the version in your lockfile. Pay special attention to new dependencies the change adds. Ask yourself whether you would have chosen that package.

Human's job: verify unfamiliar calls and new packages.
Bot's job: a dependency check can flag packages that are outdated or have known vulnerabilities, so you do not have to look each one up.

4. Do the new lines have tests, and do those tests mean anything?

This is the one that gets the least attention.

Overall coverage is a project-wide number. A pull request can add a lot of untested code and barely move it, because the old, well-tested code dilutes the result. The opposite also happens: a refactor can lower overall coverage even though the new code is fine.

What you want to know is patch coverage: of the lines this pull request changed, how many are exercised by tests? That number says much more about this specific change than the project average does.

Then check what the tests actually assert. A quick trick: flip one assertion and see whether the test still passes. If it does, the test is decoration.

// Looks like a test. Proves nothing.
test("creates a user", async () => {
  const user = await createUser({ name: "Sam" });
  expect(user).toBeDefined();
});

Human's job: read the assertions.
Bot's job: report coverage for the changed lines separately from the project total, so a gap is visible without opening a coverage report.

5. Did it copy something that already exists?

AI does not know your codebase the way you do. It often writes a new helper next to an identical one that already lives three folders away. Every copy is a place where the next bug fix has to be made twice.

Search for similar logic before approving. A new utility function should make you ask whether one already exists.

Human's job: recognize existing helpers you know about.
Bot's job: a duplication check can flag repeated blocks the pull request introduced.

6. What happens when things go wrong?

Generated code handles the happy path beautifully. Check the unhappy paths:

  • What happens with empty input or missing values?
  • What happens on a timeout or a failed network call?
  • Are errors swallowed silently? An empty catch block is a classic.
  • Does it log anything useful when it fails?

Human's job: think about failure cases.
Bot's job: a complexity check can point at functions that have grown many branches, which is where failure handling usually hides.

7. Did a secret slip in?

Agents copy examples. Sometimes an example contains something that looks like a real key, and sometimes it is one. Check for hardcoded tokens, passwords and connection strings in the diff.

Human's job: glance at config and environment changes.
Bot's job: a secrets scan on the changed lines is cheap and catches the obvious cases.

A checklist you can paste into your pull request template 

- [ ] I can state in one sentence what this change should do
- [ ] The files changed match the task
- [ ] The diff is small enough to review properly
- [ ] New imports and API calls exist in our installed versions
- [ ] New dependencies are justified, current and safe
- [ ] Changed lines have tests that fail when the code breaks
- [ ] Nothing duplicates a helper we already have
- [ ] Empty, null and failure cases are handled
- [ ] No secrets in the diff

Let a bot do the boring half

Items 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 are partly mechanical. A human reading the diff is a slow and tired way to check them, and the review energy is better spent on item 1 and on the design questions only you can answer.

DebtDraft is built for this. It is a GitHub Action that leaves one comment on each pull request with a health score across the signals above: complexity, test coverage, duplication, outdated dependencies and known-vulnerable dependencies. It also shows the changed lines on their own, so you can see what this specific pull request did, and a dashboard shows how your repository trends over time.

It is free for up to three repositories, and setup is one workflow step. If you try it, let us know what you think.

Your turn

What is the sneakiest problem you have seen in an AI-generated pull request? Share it with us in the comments.

articles.title: SlothVault: A Zero-Effort Local MCP + RAG Agent That Rewards Digital Laziness published: true
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady          ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

SlothVault is a local-first personal RAG utility built for anyone too tired or busy to manually sort, tag, and organize digital clutter.

Every day, developers and researchers accumulate messy context fragments:

  • Home lab and Wi-Fi credentials
  • Cloud subscription renewal dates and invoice amounts
  • Medical appointments and task deadlines

Most productivity guides advise spending hours building complex databases in Notion or Obsidian. SlothVault takes the lazy approach: dump your unorganized notes into a local vault and let an open-weight agent fetch what you need in seconds.

  1. Zero Manual Tagging: It ingests raw notes, credentials, and .txt files on the fly.
  2. MCP Tool Integration: Exposes standard Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool contracts (retrieve_from_vault and add_to_vault).
  3. 2-Sentence Brief: Uses local embeddings and an open-weight language model to extract the exact fact and output a concise brief.

Demo

Code 

import json
import torch
import numpy as np
import gradio as gr
from transformers import pipeline
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

# 1. Load Local Open-Weight Models
embed_model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
llm_pipeline = pipeline(
    "text-generation",
    model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct",
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16 if torch.cuda.is_available() else torch.float32,
    device_map="auto" if torch.cuda.is_available() else None
)

# 2. In-Memory Vault & Seed Data
vault_docs = [
    "WiFi Password for Home Lab is 'lazy_sloth_42'. Do not share externally.",
    "Invoice #8841 from Cloud hosting was $45.20, due on November 5th.",
    "Doctor appointment rescheduled to Friday at 4:30 PM with Dr. Sharma.",
    "Project roadmap milestone 2 requires TabPFN model benchmarking by next Tuesday."
]
vault_embeddings = embed_model.encode(vault_docs)

# 3. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Tool Functions
def mcp_retrieve_from_vault(query: str, top_k: int = 2):
    global vault_docs, vault_embeddings
    if not vault_docs:
        return []
    q_vec = embed_model.encode([query])
    scores = cosine_similarity(q_vec, vault_embeddings)[0]
    top_indices = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:top_k]
    return [{"text": vault_docs[i], "similarity_score": round(float(scores[i]), 3)} for i in top_indices]

def mcp_add_to_vault(new_text: str):
    global vault_docs, vault_embeddings
    cleaned = new_text.strip()
    if not cleaned:
        return "Empty note."
    vault_docs.append(cleaned)
    new_embedding = embed_model.encode([cleaned])
    vault_embeddings = np.vstack([vault_embeddings, new_embedding])
    return f"Added to vault. Total items: {len(vault_docs)}"

# 4. Agent Synthesis
SYSTEM_PROMPT = (
    "You are SlothVault. The user is exhausted. You have executed the MCP tool "
    "'retrieve_from_vault' and received matching records. "
    "Give the exact answer in 1-2 punchy sentences. "
    "End with a short sloth remark like 'Now go back to resting. 🦥'."
)

def sloth_agent_search(query: str):
    if not query.strip():
        return "Ask something you're too lazy to search for!"

    retrieved = mcp_retrieve_from_vault(query, top_k=2)
    context_str = "\n".join([f"- {r['text']} (Match: {r['similarity_score']})" for r in retrieved])

    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": f"Query: {query}\n\nContext:\n{context_str}"}
    ]

    res = llm_pipeline(messages, max_new_tokens=120, temperature=0.2)
    answer = res[0]["generated_text"][-1]["content"].strip()

    trace = (
        f"```
{% endraw %}
json\n"
        f"// MCP Tool Execution Trace\n"
        f'{{"tool": "retrieve_from_vault", "query": "{query}", "matches": {len(retrieved)}}}\n'
        f"
{% raw %}


\n\n"
f"Retrieved Context:\n{context_str}\n\n"
f"---\n"
f"### Sloth Answer\n{answer}"
)
return trace

def handle_upload(file_obj, raw_text):
count = 0
if file_obj is not None:
with open(file_obj.name, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore") as f:
for line in f.readlines():
if line.strip():
mcp_add_to_vault(line.strip())
count += 1
if raw_text and raw_text.strip():
mcp_add_to_vault(raw_text.strip())
count += 1
return f"Successfully ingested {count} item(s) into vault."

5. Gradio Interface

with gr.Blocks(theme=gr.themes.Soft(), title="SlothVault") as demo:
gr.Markdown("# SlothVault: Zero-Effort Local MCP + RAG Agent")
gr.Markdown("Stop organizing notes manually. Dump raw clutter and let an open-weight agent retrieve it.")

with gr.Tab(" Ask the Sloth Agent"):
    query_in = gr.Textbox(label="Ask anything:", value="What is my home lab wifi password and when is the cloud bill due?")
    search_btn = gr.Button(" Find It For Me", variant="primary")
    output_box = gr.Markdown()
    search_btn.click(fn=sloth_agent_search, inputs=query_in, outputs=output_box)

with gr.Tab(" Dump More Clutter (Add Notes)"):
    note_in = gr.Textbox(label="Paste note or snippet:", placeholder="e.g., Gate code is 8842")
    file_in = gr.File(label="Upload .txt file", file_types=[".txt"])
    add_btn = gr.Button(" Ingest Without Organizing")
    status_box = gr.Markdown()
    add_btn.click(fn=handle_upload, inputs=[file_in, note_in], outputs=status_box)

demo.launch(share=True)

How I Built It
SlothVault combines open-weight models, dense semantic retrieval, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP):

Standardized MCP Tool Contracts: Instead of building an ad-hoc search script, the data operations implement retrieve_from_vault and add_to_vault tool definitions, ensuring compatibility with standard agent frameworks.

Fast Local Vector Search: sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeds text into 384-dimensional vectors. Cosine similarity matching retrieves the top-ranked context in milliseconds without a heavy external vector database.

Local Open-Weight Reasoning: Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct synthesizes the retrieved chunks on-device, extracting precise facts and avoiding generative hallucinations.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?
Absolute Privacy: Personal notes, Wi-Fi credentials, medical reminders, and invoices never leave the machine. Running inference locally keeps sensitive personal data off third-party servers.

Zero Operating Cost: Powered by open weights, the agent runs entirely free of token limits, monthly subscriptions, or cloud API paywalls.

Offline Reliability: Because the models run on-device, the agent functions normally on a laptop even without an internet connection.

Prize Categories
Top Prize: Slow and Steady ($250 USD)

articles.title: The GUID That Sorts Itself (Until It Doesn't)
articles.description: Version 7 GUIDs give you time-ordered keys and fix the random-GUID index fragmentation problem. Then I generated 100,000 in a burst and found exactly where 'sortable' stops meaning 'ordered'.
articles.body_html:
I was looking at an index on a table whose primary key is a uniqueidentifier, and the fragmentation number was ugly. Every insert dropped a fresh Guid.NewGuid() into a random spot in the key range, so the B-tree was constantly splitting pages to make room in the middle. Classic random-GUID problem. I'd read about Version 7 GUIDs fixing this, and .NET has Guid.CreateVersion7() now, so I figured I'd swap it in and move on.

Then I got curious about how far I could actually trust the sort. So I did the thing I always do: wrote the smallest program that would tell me, and ran it instead of guessing.

What v4 keys look like when you line them up

Here's the baseline. Make six ordinary GUIDs a couple milliseconds apart, print them in the order I made them, then sort them and ask if the sorted order matches:

var v4Keys = new List<Guid>();
for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++)
{
    v4Keys.Add(Guid.NewGuid());
    Thread.Sleep(2);
}

var v4Sorted = v4Keys.OrderBy(g => g).ToList();
Console.WriteLine($"Sorted == creation order? {v4Sorted.SequenceEqual(v4Keys)}");

a23b61f1-613d-464a-a2e2-7ac3ccf522e0
ebd6f78a-afbc-42de-9450-cdee1416c9e9
3001f306-6a01-4556-b338-b3649735a280
dcf56d17-4dd3-4087-8409-9958e0e17f61
a06dcf69-ccc2-4642-b610-b21bfd05b99e
b4da4432-b310-46fc-877d-3bf6aa89de0d
Sorted == creation order? False

No surprise. A v4 GUID is 122 random bits. The value you get has nothing to do with when you asked for it, which is exactly why it scatters across the index.

v7 keys carry the time in their front teeth

A Version 7 GUID puts a 48-bit Unix-millisecond timestamp in the high bits and fills the rest with randomness. Same loop, same two-millisecond gaps, swap the factory:

var v7Keys = new List<Guid>();
for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++)
{
    v7Keys.Add(Guid.CreateVersion7());
    Thread.Sleep(2);
}

01a17719-db51-7dc3-b700-0ff42fff55da  @ 07:25:45.681
01a17719-db54-713b-adec-96911e0ab1fe  @ 07:25:45.684
01a17719-db56-7379-9292-eedae31b7e54  @ 07:25:45.686
01a17719-db58-764f-b15b-faa65bb7ff23  @ 07:25:45.688
01a17719-db5a-775e-a3b6-e12cee035baf  @ 07:25:45.690
01a17719-db5c-7722-8037-9f652b6883f6  @ 07:25:45.692
Sorted == creation order? True

Look at the left edge of each one. The prefix climbs in lockstep with the clock, so sorting the bytes sorts by time. New keys land at the end of the range instead of the middle, and that's the whole point for a database: inserts append, pages stop splitting.

And that timestamp isn't a party trick, you can read it straight back out of the key. The byte layout is big-endian for the RFC, so I ask for the bytes in that order and pull the first six:

static DateTimeOffset ReadTimestamp(Guid guid)
{
    Span<byte> bytes = stackalloc byte[16];
    guid.TryWriteBytes(bytes, bigEndian: true, out _);
    Span<byte> ms = stackalloc byte[8];
    bytes[..6].CopyTo(ms[2..]);   // 48-bit value, right-aligned in a long
    long unixMs = BinaryPrimitives.ReadInt64BigEndian(ms);
    return DateTimeOffset.FromUnixTimeMilliseconds(unixMs);
}

That bigEndian: true matters. Guid stores its first three fields in little-endian internally, so the default ToByteArray() gives you a jumbled prefix and the timestamp comes out as nonsense. The overload that takes the flag is the one you want.

The part the blog posts skip

Here's where I stopped trusting the word "sortable" and made it earn it. Those sleeps above are doing a lot of work, each key got its own millisecond. Real inserts don't wait politely. So I generated a hundred thousand of them as fast as the loop would go and asked the same question:

const int burst = 100_000;
var sameMs = new Guid[burst];
for (int i = 0; i < burst; i++)
    sameMs[i] = Guid.CreateVersion7();

var byValue = sameMs.OrderBy(g => g).ToArray();
bool matches = byValue.AsSpan().SequenceEqual(sameMs);

Burst of 100,000 v7 GUIDs took 71.8 ms
  spanned 55 distinct millisecond bucket(s)
  sorting recovers exact creation order? False

False. A hundred thousand keys fell into 55 millisecond buckets, so roughly eighteen hundred of them share each bucket, and inside a bucket the ordering bits are random. Sorting gets you to the right millisecond and then shrugs. I printed a pair to see it plainly:

Same millisecond, created a then b, but b < a byte-wise:
  a (first)  01a17719-db60-79bc-84dd-1b62234a3abb
  b (second) 01a17719-db60-753f-90e6-9be4edb208b7

Created a first, b second, same millisecond, and b sorts ahead of a. That's not a bug. .NET 10's implementation doesn't add a monotonic counter in the low bits, so two keys born in the same millisecond can come back in either order. (The spec leaves room for a counter; this runtime doesn't use one.)

This is a container, not a lab bench, and the 71.8 ms will be different on your box. The number I care about is 55 buckets, because it says the thing that matters: at insert speed, "sorted" means sorted to the millisecond, nothing finer.

So where I actually landed

For database keys, v7 is a straight upgrade over v4 and I'd reach for it by default now. The index locality is real, and getting a creation timestamp baked into the key for free is a nice bonus when you're squinting at rows in production. My one caution: don't let "time-ordered" slide into "ordered." If you need to know which of two rows was inserted first, and they might land in the same millisecond, you still need a real sequence or an identity column. The GUID won't settle that argument, and it'll look like it might, which is worse.

Want to see it on your own hardware? Here's the whole thing in one file, Program.cs, targeting net10.0 (it runs fine on .NET 9 too). No packages.

using System.Buffers.Binary;
using System.Diagnostics;

Console.WriteLine($"Running on .NET {Environment.Version}\n");

var v4Keys = new List<Guid>();
for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) { v4Keys.Add(Guid.NewGuid()); Thread.Sleep(2); }
Console.WriteLine("v4 in creation order:");
foreach (var g in v4Keys) Console.WriteLine($"  {g}");
var v4Sorted = v4Keys.OrderBy(g => g).ToList();
Console.WriteLine($"  Sorted == creation order? {v4Sorted.SequenceEqual(v4Keys)}\n");

var v7Keys = new List<Guid>();
for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) { v7Keys.Add(Guid.CreateVersion7()); Thread.Sleep(2); }
Console.WriteLine("v7 in creation order:");
foreach (var g in v7Keys) Console.WriteLine($"  {g}  @ {ReadTimestamp(g):HH:mm:ss.fff}");
var v7Sorted = v7Keys.OrderBy(g => g).ToList();
Console.WriteLine($"  Sorted == creation order? {v7Sorted.SequenceEqual(v7Keys)}\n");

const int burst = 100_000;
var sameMs = new Guid[burst];
var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
for (int i = 0; i < burst; i++) sameMs[i] = Guid.CreateVersion7();
sw.Stop();
int buckets = sameMs.Select(ReadTimestamp).Distinct().Count();
var byValue = sameMs.OrderBy(g => g).ToArray();
bool matches = byValue.AsSpan().SequenceEqual(sameMs);
Console.WriteLine($"Burst of {burst:N0} v7 GUIDs took {sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds:F1} ms");
Console.WriteLine($"  spanned {buckets} distinct millisecond bucket(s)");
Console.WriteLine($"  sorting recovers exact creation order? {matches}\n");

for (int i = 1; i < burst; i++)
{
    if (ReadTimestamp(sameMs[i]) == ReadTimestamp(sameMs[i - 1]) &&
        sameMs[i].CompareTo(sameMs[i - 1]) < 0)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Same millisecond, created a then b, but b < a byte-wise:");
        Console.WriteLine($"  a (first)  {sameMs[i - 1]}");
        Console.WriteLine($"  b (second) {sameMs[i]}");
        break;
    }
}

static DateTimeOffset ReadTimestamp(Guid guid)
{
    Span<byte> bytes = stackalloc byte[16];
    guid.TryWriteBytes(bytes, bigEndian: true, out _);
    Span<byte> ms = stackalloc byte[8];
    bytes[..6].CopyTo(ms[2..]);
    long unixMs = BinaryPrimitives.ReadInt64BigEndian(ms);
    return DateTimeOffset.FromUnixTimeMilliseconds(unixMs);
}

Have you moved any tables over to v7 keys yet, or are you still sitting on sequential integers? Curious what the fragmentation looked like before and after if you have.

— still benchmarking things nobody asked me to measure
