articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Ever since I bought my first computer, I have had one annoying problem: messy files. I am a bit lazy myself and I hate boring tasks, so I built sloth-tidy.

sloth-tidy is a small Python tool that tidies a messy folder for me. A local open model (Gemma, running through Ollama) reads each file, picks a suitable folder for it, and gives it a clean, readable name. Uni files go to Uni, receipts go to Receipts, tickets go to Travel, and you can add your own folders. This makes my life much easier, especially when I need to find a document for an application and every file has a messy name.

It also does a few things I find really useful as a student:

  • Calendar reminders: if a document contains a future date (a flight ticket, a reservation, an exam), it offers to create a reminder.
  • Duplicates: if two files are identical, it asks which one to keep, so the folder stays clean. Nothing is deleted; the other copy just moves to a Duplicates folder.
  • Undo: it keeps a log of every move, so if I do not like the result, I can undo the last run.

Demo

Code

SarpDoruk06 / sloth-tidy

A lazy local file tidier powered by Gemma and Ollama for Hacktoberfest

sloth-tidy 🦥

A lazy, fully local file tidier. Point it at a messy folder (like Downloads) and a local open-weight model (Gemma, via Ollama) decides which folder each file belongs in and gives it a readable name. No cloud, no API key, no account.

Built for the DEV / Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 3: "Slow and Steady".

What it does

  • Sorts files into folders such as Uni, Receipts, Travel. Photos, installers and archives are sorted by file type without using the model.
  • Offers calendar reminders. If a document mentions a future date (a flight, an exam a deadline), it asks "Create a calendar reminder? [y/N]". Say yes and it makes a .ics file with an alert one day before and opens it in your calendar app.
  • Finds duplicates. If two files are byte-for-byte identical it asks which to keep The other goes to Duplicates/. Nothing is ever deleted.
  • …
View on GitHub

Code: https://github.com/SarpDoruk06/sloth-tidy

How I Built It

  • Model: I used Gemma (gemma3:4b) running locally through Ollama.
  • How it works: Basically, files like photos and installers are sorted by extension, so no model is needed. For documents, the first page of text goes to Gemma, which answers in JSON: a folder, a short name, and an optional event. I check every answer before anything moves: unknown folders become "Other", and past or invalid dates are dropped.
  • Duplicates: SHA-256 hashes, only for files of the same size.
  • Reminders: I had the idea to add reminders to make the tool even more useful. The model only suggests an event, because creating a calendar entry every time it sees a future date would be annoying and risky. A standard .ics file is created only after I say yes, so a misread date never reaches my calendar on its own. I wanted the tool to be lazy but still under my control.
  • Safety: I wanted to know what the tool will do before it does it, and to never regret anything. So dry run is the default, nothing is ever overwritten or deleted, and --undo reverts the last run. In my demo test, undo brought back 9 of 9 files. This was the case for most of the test runs.
  • Tests: 21 tests with pytest, and GitHub Actions runs them on every push. I also tested the tool on my own folders. In one of the tests, on the first run, a folder with 47 files went through smoothly, and by my last test I had brought the response time down from 301.8 s to 244.2 s. On a second folder of 25 files it took 130.8 s: 8 files sorted by extension, 12 by the model, 5 duplicates, and 2 scans without readable text.
  • AI help: I built this together with a little help from an AI assistant, Claude. I did a small part of the coding and most of the debugging on my own. I decided what the tool should do, tested everything on my own files, and kept noting down response times, file types, errors and bugs. The problems I found:
    • undo skipped files after an old log was left in the folder
    • a scanned PDF with no readable text, which the model could only judge by its file name
    • a payment receipt that landed in Travel instead of Receipts
    • two reminders for the same trip (a ticket and its receipt). I chose to show both with a warning instead of merging them quietly.

The undo problem and the double reminders are fixed. The scans without text are a limit of the tool, because it has no OCR.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • My files stay mine. Important things such as receipts, travel tickets and uni documents never leave my laptop. If you ask why this matters to me: my downloads folder contains documents with personal details, and I would not upload them to a server I do not control. This way I keep full control.
  • It works offline and costs nothing after the one-time model download. For me this is the major upside with the ridiculous prices of some closed APIs these days. Plus, it helps you learn some coding along the way. No account, no API key, no subscription. For a student this means huge savings and being able to learn new things. Also not worrying about managing your account when you have midterms coming.
  • I can swap the model. For this project I only focused on Gemma and didn't use any other models. I tried some versions of it for testing though. The good thing is that sloth-tidy has a built-in --model option, so anyone can try another open model without changing the code.
  • Honest limits. Small models make mistakes. Even when you spend countless hours on a project to perfect it there are bound to be some mistakes. I encountered some myself, such as a payment receipt going to the Travel folder, or some scans without readable text. Another was that in one of my tests I had some python files and I couldn't manage to make the tool sort them into the Uni folder. This is precisely why dry run, undo and confirmation exist.

The Lazy Payoff

I tested sloth-tidy on copies of my own folders.

  • Demo folder, 9 files: All 9 were sorted correctly, one duplicate was found, and undo brought everything back. The dry run took 61.9 s. Two reminder ideas were found (an exam and a train ticket) and I accepted one. The files were simple, so the time saved was small: I guess it would take me 2 to 3 minutes by hand.

  • 47 files: My first big test went through smoothly. Over my tests I brought the response time down from 301.8 s to 244.2 s. Normally going through 47 files, looking to each ones content and also adding a reminder if there needs to be one would take more than 20 to 25 minutes. So I would say this program saves me at least 15 minutes by doing a 20-minute job in 4 minutes. I can also do something else while it runs.

  • 25 files: Sorted in 130.8 s. 8 files were sorted by file type, 12 by Gemma, 5 were duplicates, and 2 were scans without readable text, so the model could only judge them by file name.

  • 15 messy files: All 15 were sorted correctly, and undo brought everything back. I cannot say for sure how much time it saved me, because the files were not very complicated, only one reminder was needed and 15 files is not really enough to call a folder messy. It took the program about 90 s and I guess it would take me around 3-4 minutes manually.

  • What went wrong: In tests that include many files some were sorted wrongly. A payment receipt landed in Travel instead of Receipts. I left this in the post on purpose: a small local model is not perfect and can still get a messy real-world file wrong, and that is why dry run, undo and confirmation exist. Although this specific issue was later fixed.

It also has a --watch mode: it tidies the folder in the background every few minutes, so I do not have to remember to run it and I can do something else while it runs.

Sloth-tidy is not perfect: it cannot read scanned PDFs yet (OCR is the next thing I would like to add), and a small model sometimes picks the wrong folder. But it already does what I wanted: it tidies my folders while I do something else, and my files never leave my laptop.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma: the whole tool runs on Gemma (gemma3:4b) locally through Ollama. It uses Gemma to read the documents, pick a folder, suggest a clearer name, and find dates for reminders. Nothing ever leaves my laptop

articles.title: What is props reactivity loss in Vue and how to avoid it?
articles.description: Hey folks!  Today, I would like to share with you a problem I encountered recently in my project and...
articles.body_html:
Hey folks!

Today, I would like to share with you a problem I encountered recently in my project and how I overcome it. I will get to the point to explain the problem quicky, what are the possible solutions to solve and what we decided to go with and why - without unnecessary content polution but certain Intelligence ;)

Let me know your thoughts!

Disclaimer

I wasn't writing for some time as I needed to rethink what I want to share with you and in what form.

Basically, all my recent posts/articles were somehow AI created - either fully or highly assisted. And honestly, I don't feel ok with that. I believe what made you stay with my blog is the feeling that the author is authentic - that the problems I am solving are real and based on the everyday work with the framework I love - Vue.

So, I am changing a form. I will publish hand written (obviously not perfect) articles that will cover problems or real life case studies I have encountered a week before - no more AI generated content I promise ;)

What I believe made you stay with my blog is authenticity - I was writing about problems I was encountering everyday as I was not able to find an answer for it. This form I would like to continue - and I hope you will like it! :)

Problem

One of the developers came back to me recently saying: I have created a new feature package/module for our project (that is independent from other domains) and I encountered this problem while following the previously agreed approach:

Destructuring the `props` will cause the value to lose reactivity.

The code was looking more or less like following:

<script setup lang="ts">
const props = defineProps<{
  apiClient: Client
}>()

const result = getProduct(apiClient, key)
// Destructuring the `props` will cause the value to lose reactivity.
</script>

And he then asked: What should I do?

Solutions

We have considered three available solutions:

  • Use the toValue helper from Vue - this was good as temporary solution to hide the eslint error but we didn't want to go with this approach as our final option
  • The second option was to wrap the prop inside a computed property or watcher like: 
    watch(() => props.apiClient, () => {
      console.log(props.apiClient)
    })

But we didn't like this solution either as we basically were assuming that the apiClient can change - while in our case the apiClient is a static dependency.

  • Pass the apiClient via provide/inject instead. This pattern can be used to provide both reactive and static values to your app.

Selected approach

We have selected the third option as it looked the best from the architectural point of view. We have a static apiClient that we want to provide to all consumers in our app that can inject them just in the moment they need it. This also helps with the concept of prop drilling as we don't need to pass the prop in a nested tree.

But it also comes with some drawbacks such as less visible interface of individual packages externally that we wanted to achieve in the first place.

You have a better approach? Something I missed? Share it in the comments! :)

articles.title: My VS Code setup went from 47 extensions to 6. My productivity went up.
articles.description: I counted my VS Code extensions. There were 47. My editor took 8 seconds to start, lagged when I...
articles.body_html:
I counted my VS Code extensions. There were 47. My editor took 8 seconds to start, lagged when I typed, and crashed once a week. I disabled 41 of them and kept 6. Here is what happened.

The problem

Extension creep is gradual. You install a formatter, then a linter, then a theme, then a snippet pack, then a language support extension for a framework you tried once and never used again. Each one seems small. Each one adds startup time, memory usage, and editor complexity.

My 47 extensions included:

  • 5 formatters (Prettier, ESLint, Stylelint, Beautify, Rustfmt)
  • 4 language packs (Python, Go, Rust, Java, only Python was active)
  • 3 themes (one in use, two installed "to try later")
  • 6 snippet packs (React, Vue, Python, Docker, Git, and a generic HTML one)
  • 4 Git extensions (GitLens, Git Graph, GitHub Pull Requests, Git History)
  • 3 AI extensions (GitHub Copilot, Codeium, Tabnine, all disabled in favor of Cursor)
  • 22 others (Docker, YAML, TOML, markdown preview, CSV viewer, path intellisense, import cost, indent rainbow, bracket pair colorizer, and more)

Most of these I had installed once and forgotten about. They were running on every startup, consuming memory, registering commands, and contributing to the status bar.

What I kept

I went through each extension and asked: "Have I used this in the last week?" If the answer was no, I disabled it. Here is what survived:

1. Prettier. Code formatting. I use it on every file. Non-negotiable.

2. ESLint. Linting. Same as Prettier, I use it constantly. The two work together.

3. GitLens. I use the blame and diff features daily. The rest of GitLens (code lens, file history, commit search) I could live without, but the blame view alone justifies the extension.

4. Astro. Language support for Astro, which is my primary framework. Without it, .astro files are unstyled HTML.

5. Tailwind CSS IntelliSense. Autocomplete for Tailwind classes. I write Tailwind every day. Without this, I am guessing at class names.

6. Error Lens. Shows errors and warnings inline instead of requiring a hover. It is a small UX improvement that saves me hundreds of micro-interactions per day.

That is it. Six extensions.

What happened

Startup time: 8 seconds to 1.5 seconds. The difference is immediately noticeable. I open and close the editor many times a day, and the 6.5 second saving compounds.

Memory usage: 1.2 GB to 380 MB. VS Code went from being the heaviest application on my machine to being lighter than my browser. The lag when typing in large files disappeared.

Crashes: once a week to zero in six weeks. I cannot prove causation, but the correlation is strong. Extension conflicts are a known cause of VS Code instability, and removing 41 of them eliminated a lot of potential conflicts.

Productivity: up, measurably. I was spending time managing extensions: updating them, configuring them, disabling ones that conflicted, and debugging issues caused by interaction between them. That time is gone. The editor does what I need and gets out of the way.

What I learned about extension creep

Extensions are not free. Each one adds to startup time, memory footprint, and editor complexity. The cost is invisible until you remove them and feel the difference.

You do not use most of your extensions. 41 out of 47 had not been used in the last week. Some had not been used in months. They were running anyway.

The best extensions are the ones you forget you have. Prettier, ESLint, Error Lens: these work silently. They do not have popups, side panels, or status bar clutter. They do their job and disappear.

AI extensions are redundant when you use an AI editor. I was running Copilot, Codeium, and Tabnine inside VS Code while also using Cursor (which has its own AI). The AI extensions were disabled but still loaded. Removing them freed memory and removed a source of confusion about which AI was active.

The 2026 editor landscape

The choice in 2026 is not "which extensions should I install." It is "which editor should I use." The landscape:

  • VS Code remains the default. The extension ecosystem is the largest. With a minimal setup, it is fast and reliable.
  • Cursor is VS Code with AI built in. If you are paying for an AI assistant, Cursor replaces the need for AI extensions.
  • Zed is the performance option. Rust-native, fast startup, built-in collaboration. Smaller extension ecosystem.
  • JetBrains (WebStorm, IntelliJ) is the heavy option. Built-in tooling for everything, but higher memory footprint and per-seat licensing.

My current setup is Cursor (which is VS Code under the hood) with the same 6 extensions. The AI features are built into the editor, so I do not need AI extensions. The 6 extensions I kept are the ones that do work the AI cannot do: format my code, lint it, show Astro syntax, autocomplete Tailwind classes, and display errors inline.

If you want to try this

  1. Open your extensions tab. Sort by "installed."
  2. For each extension, ask: "Have I used this in the last week?"
  3. Disable everything where the answer is no. Do not uninstall yet, just disable.
  4. Work for a week. If you need an extension you disabled, re-enable it.
  5. After a week, uninstall everything that is still disabled.
  6. Measure your startup time before and after. The difference is your motivation to keep it lean.

The temptation to install will return. Every blog post about "10 VS Code extensions you must have" will add to your list. The discipline is not "never install." It is "install, try, and remove if you do not use it within a week."

articles.title: GCS Write Errors Ran for 12.5 Hours in us-central1. Spool Uploads to Disk, Drain Later
articles.description: Google's Oct 8 GCS incident listed no workaround. Build a bounded on-disk upload spool in Node that fills during an outage and drains with jitter.
articles.body_html:
• Book: System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

On October 8, 2026, Google Cloud Storage in us-central1 spent twelve and a half hours returning errors and timeouts on writes. Google's incident report puts the impact from 04:00 to 16:30 US/Pacific, which is 11:00 to 23:30 UTC. Every status update posted during the day carried the same line under Workaround: "None at this time."

Then it came back. The final report adds a second window on October 9, 04:05 to 09:46 Pacific, in the us-central1-b zone, for a total of 18 hours and 11 minutes.

If your service writes user uploads or exports straight to a bucket in that region, that was up to 18 hours in which any write could come back as a 503 or hang until your timeout fired, and the writes that did succeed were slow. Google's load balancer is not yours to fix; what your process does with the bytes when the bucket says no is.

The answer fits in plain Node. Failed writes land in a bounded spool on local disk; a drainer pushes them back with jittered retries once the bucket recovers; a gauge shows how deep the backlog is. It all runs against a fake bucket you can break on command, so you can watch the spool fill and empty.

What the report says, and why your client's retries run out

The report is specific. A "traffic sorting optimization configuration update" to the Cloud Storage load-balancing layer bypassed capacity-aware routing and pushed write traffic onto low-capacity backend nodes, which ran out of resources. A separate metadata database issue added errors on top. Engineers tried to add emergency capacity, but per the report "this was blocked by systemic regional capacity limits." The October 9 recurrence came from an incomplete rollback of an upload planner feature.

What clients saw: "Customers primarily observed HTTP 503 UNAVAILABLE errors on WriteObject operations and client-side timeouts." Reads were hit less. Other regions were fine.

The official client's answer to a 503 is on the Cloud Storage retry strategy page, which lists 408, 429 and 5xx responses, plus socket timeouts, as retryable, and recommends exponential backoff with jitter. The Node.js defaults on that page: 3 retries, a 1-second initial wait, a multiplier of 2, a 64-second maximum wait, and a 600-second overall deadline. Uploads are only retried automatically when they are idempotent, meaning you passed an ifGenerationMatch precondition.

So the client gives up after three retries, or ten minutes at the very most. Against a twelve-hour outage, in-request retries are a rounding error. Past that point, the bytes have to live somewhere other than the request, and they have to survive a process restart, because over twelve hours you will deploy, scale, or crash at least once.


When the bucket stops accepting writes, the bytes need a place to wait that outlives the request.

A bounded spool on disk

The spool is a directory. One file per pending object. Each file holds a one-line JSON header with the object name, then the raw bytes. Three rules keep it honest:

  • Write to a temp file, then rename. A crash mid-write leaves a .tmp file that init() deletes, never a half-written entry the drainer would choke on.
  • Cap both file count and bytes. A spool without a cap turns a storage outage into a full-disk outage on your own host.
  • Reserve capacity before the first await. Twenty concurrent failures must not all pass the cap check and then all write. 
// spool.mjs
import {
  mkdir, readdir, readFile, rename, rm, stat, writeFile,
} from 'node:fs/promises';
import { join } from 'node:path';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

export class SpoolFullError extends Error {}

export class Spool {
  constructor(dir, { maxBytes, maxFiles }) {
    this.dir = dir;
    this.maxBytes = maxBytes;
    this.maxFiles = maxFiles;
    this.bytes = 0;
    this.files = 0;
  }

  async init() {
    await mkdir(this.dir, { recursive: true });
    for (const f of await readdir(this.dir)) {
      const path = join(this.dir, f);
      if (f.endsWith('.tmp')) {
        await rm(path, { force: true });
      } else if (f.endsWith('.spool')) {
        this.bytes += (await stat(path)).size;
        this.files += 1;
      }
    }
  }

  async put(name, data) {
    const head = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ name }) + '\n');
    const body = Buffer.concat([head, data]);
    if (this.files + 1 > this.maxFiles ||
        this.bytes + body.length > this.maxBytes) {
      throw new SpoolFullError(`spool full: ${this.files}`);
    }
    // reserve first, so concurrent puts respect the cap
    this.files += 1;
    this.bytes += body.length;
    const id = `${Date.now()}-${randomUUID()}`;
    const final = join(this.dir, `${id}.spool`);
    const tmp = `${final}.tmp`;
    try {
      await writeFile(tmp, body, { flush: true });
      await rename(tmp, final);
    } catch (err) {
      this.files -= 1;
      this.bytes -= body.length;
      await rm(tmp, { force: true });
      throw err;
    }
  }

  async list() {
    const names = await readdir(this.dir);
    return names.filter((f) => f.endsWith('.spool')).sort();
  }

  async oldestAgeMs() {
    const [first] = await this.list();
    return first ? Date.now() - Number(first.split('-')[0]) : 0;
  }

  async oldest() {
    const [first] = await this.list();
    if (!first) return null;
    const path = join(this.dir, first);
    const buf = await readFile(path);
    const nl = buf.indexOf(10); // the header ends at the first \n
    const { name } = JSON.parse(buf.subarray(0, nl).toString());
    const data = buf.subarray(nl + 1);
    return { path, name, data, size: buf.length };
  }

  async remove(entry) {
    await rm(entry.path);
    this.files -= 1;
    this.bytes -= entry.size;
  }
}

flush: true makes writeFile call sync() on the handle before closing it, so the bytes are on disk before the rename publishes the entry. The option landed in Node v21.0.0 and v20.10.0 per the Node fs docs. File names start with Date.now(), so a lexical sort gives you oldest-first, and the age of the oldest entry falls out of the name without opening the file. JSON.stringify escapes newlines inside the object name, so the first raw \n in the file always ends the header.

The upload path is short. Try the bucket with a timeout. If the failure is one a retry could fix, spool it. If the spool is full, put throws SpoolFullError and your caller decides what to do, which is the backpressure: return a 503 to your own client, pause a consumer, stop reading from a queue. The one thing you must not do is drop the write silently.

// uploader.mjs
const WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS = 2_000;
const NET = ['ECONNRESET', 'ETIMEDOUT', 'EPIPE'];

export function isRetryable(err) {
  if (err?.name === 'TimeoutError') return true;
  if (NET.includes(err?.code)) return true;
  const status = Number(err?.code);
  return status === 408 || status === 429 || status >= 500;
}

export async function upload(bucket, spool, name, data) {
  try {
    await bucket.write(name, data, {
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS),
    });
    return 'stored';
  } catch (err) {
    if (!isRetryable(err)) throw err;
    await spool.put(name, data); // may throw SpoolFullError
    return 'spooled';
  }
}

The retryable set mirrors Google's list: 408, 429, 5xx, and timeouts. A 403 or 404 is a bug in your code or config, and spooling it would hide that bug for hours. AbortSignal.timeout() gives you a signal that aborts after the given milliseconds with a TimeoutError as its reason, which is what isRetryable checks for.

Drain with full jitter

The drainer is one loop. Take the oldest entry, try to write it, delete it on success. On a retryable failure, sleep a random amount between zero and an exponentially growing ceiling. That is the "full jitter" variant from Marc Brooker's Exponential Backoff and Jitter post on the AWS Architecture Blog. When a region comes back, every client that spooled is about to retry at once. Randomized sleeps spread that herd out instead of hitting the recovering backend in synchronized waves.

// drainer.mjs
import { isRetryable } from './uploader.mjs';

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

export async function drain(bucket, spool, opts = {}) {
  const {
    baseMs = 250, capMs = 30_000, idleMs = 1_000,
    timeoutMs = 5_000, signal,
  } = opts;
  let failures = 0;
  while (!signal?.aborted) {
    const entry = await spool.oldest();
    if (!entry) {
      await sleep(idleMs);
      continue;
    }
    try {
      await bucket.write(entry.name, entry.data, {
        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
      });
      await spool.remove(entry);
      failures = 0;
    } catch (err) {
      if (!isRetryable(err)) throw err;
      failures += 1;
      const ceiling = Math.min(capMs, baseMs * 2 ** failures);
      await sleep(Math.random() * ceiling); // full jitter
    }
  }
}

One drainer per process, writing one entry at a time, is deliberately slow. A recovering storage backend is the worst place to aim a burst. If your backlog is large enough that serial draining takes too long, run a small fixed number of these loops over disjoint entries, not a Promise.all over the whole directory.


Full jitter: each retry waits a random slice of a growing window, so recovering clients don't arrive in lockstep.

The real bucket adapter has one more task beyond calling the client: make the write safe to repeat. A write that timed out on your side may still have landed on Google's side. With ifGenerationMatch: 0, the request preconditions docs say the write only succeeds if no live object with that name exists, and fails with 412 Precondition Failed otherwise. For an object name that is unique per upload, a 412 on a retry means "your earlier attempt worked," so the adapter treats it as success. The preconditionOpts shape is the one Google's Node upload sample uses.

// gcs-bucket.mjs
import { Storage } from '@google-cloud/storage';

function abortable(promise, signal) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    if (signal.aborted) return reject(signal.reason);
    signal.addEventListener(
      'abort', () => reject(signal.reason), { once: true },
    );
    promise.then(resolve, reject);
  });
}

export class GcsBucket {
  constructor(bucketName) {
    this.bucket = new Storage().bucket(bucketName);
  }

  async write(name, data, { signal }) {
    const save = this.bucket.file(name).save(data, {
      resumable: false,
      preconditionOpts: { ifGenerationMatch: 0 },
    });
    try {
      await abortable(save, signal);
    } catch (err) {
      if (err?.code === 412) return; // an earlier try landed
      throw err;
    }
  }
}

abortable stops your code from waiting. It does not cancel the HTTP request underneath, which is why the adapter sends the precondition: the abandoned request can still succeed later, and the next attempt has to cope with that. The status-on-err.code check matches how the client's ApiError carries the HTTP status. Confirm it against the client version you pin, because a wrong check here turns every successful retry into a 412 that stops the drainer, with the entry still on disk.

Watch it fill and drain

The fake bucket fails on command. While failing is true, half its writes throw a 503 and the other half hang until the caller's timeout fires, which matches the two symptoms in Google's report.

// fake-bucket.mjs
export class FakeBucket {
  objects = new Map();
  failing = false;

  async write(name, data, { signal }) {
    if (this.failing) {
      if (Math.random() < 0.5) {
        const err = new Error('503 UNAVAILABLE');
        err.code = 503;
        throw err;
      }
      await new Promise((_, reject) => {
        if (signal.aborted) return reject(signal.reason);
        signal.addEventListener(
          'abort', () => reject(signal.reason), { once: true },
        );
      });
    }
    this.objects.set(name, Buffer.from(data));
  }
}

The metrics endpoint exposes the three numbers you will alert on, in the Prometheus text exposition format. No client library needed.

// metrics.mjs
import { createServer } from 'node:http';

export function serveMetrics(spool, port = 9464) {
  return createServer(async (req, res) => {
    if (req.url !== '/metrics') return res.writeHead(404).end();
    const age = (await spool.oldestAgeMs()) / 1000;
    res.writeHead(200, {
      'content-type': 'text/plain; version=0.0.4',
    });
    res.end([
      '# TYPE upload_spool_files gauge',
      `upload_spool_files ${spool.files}`,
      '# TYPE upload_spool_bytes gauge',
      `upload_spool_bytes ${spool.bytes}`,
      '# TYPE upload_spool_oldest_age_seconds gauge',
      `upload_spool_oldest_age_seconds ${age}`,
      '',
    ].join('\n'));
  }).listen(port);
}

The demo produces 50 writes a second, breaks the bucket from second 2 to second 8, and stops producing at second 10. The spool is capped at 200 files, which a six-second outage at that rate overflows on purpose, so you also see backpressure kick in.

// demo.mjs  (Node 20.10+; run: node demo.mjs)
import { FakeBucket } from './fake-bucket.mjs';
import { Spool, SpoolFullError } from './spool.mjs';
import { upload } from './uploader.mjs';
import { drain } from './drainer.mjs';
import { serveMetrics } from './metrics.mjs';

const bucket = new FakeBucket();
const spool = new Spool('./spool-data', {
  maxBytes: 5 * 1024 * 1024,
  maxFiles: 200,
});
await spool.init();

const stop = new AbortController();
const drainer = drain(bucket, spool, {
  signal: stop.signal, capMs: 2_000,
});
const metrics = serveMetrics(spool);

let n = 0;
const counts = { stored: 0, spooled: 0, rejected: 0 };
const producer = setInterval(async () => {
  const name = `events/${n++}.json`;
  const data = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ n, at: Date.now() }));
  try {
    counts[await upload(bucket, spool, name, data)] += 1;
  } catch (err) {
    if (!(err instanceof SpoolFullError)) throw err;
    counts.rejected += 1;
  }
}, 20);

const report = setInterval(() => {
  console.log(
    `depth=${spool.files} in_bucket=${bucket.objects.size}`,
    JSON.stringify(counts),
  );
}, 500);

setTimeout(() => { bucket.failing = true; }, 2_000);
setTimeout(() => { bucket.failing = false; }, 8_000);
setTimeout(() => clearInterval(producer), 10_000);
setTimeout(async () => {
  stop.abort();
  clearInterval(report);
  metrics.close();
  await drainer;
  console.log('final depth', spool.files);
}, 20_000);

What to look for in the log lines: depth sits at 0 for two seconds, climbs once the bucket breaks, hits the 200 cap, and rejected starts counting. After second 8 the drainer's next attempt succeeds, its failure counter resets, and depth falls back to 0. On a clean run, the number to check at the end is that in_bucket equals stored + spooled: everything the spool accepted made it to the bucket, and everything it refused was reported to the caller, not lost. While it runs, curl localhost:9464/metrics shows the gauges move. Kill the process mid-outage and start it again, and init() picks the backlog up from disk.

Alert on the age, not only the depth. A deep spool that is draining is fine. A shallow spool whose oldest entry is two hours old means the drainer is stuck.

- alert: UploadSpoolStuck
  expr: upload_spool_oldest_age_seconds > 900
  for: 5m
- alert: UploadSpoolNearlyFull
  expr: upload_spool_bytes > 0.8 * 5242880
  for: 2m

Where this stops helping

The spool needs a disk that survives the process. On Cloud Run, the container contract says the writable filesystem "is an in-memory file system, so writing to it uses the instance's memory," and that data written to it "doesn't persist when the instance stops." A spool there eats your memory limit and dies with the instance. Same story for a Kubernetes emptyDir when the pod is deleted. You want a persistent volume, or a VM disk.

Ordering is not preserved. While the spool drains, fresh writes go straight to the bucket and overtake older spooled ones. If a consumer depends on write order, route every write through the spool whenever it is non-empty.

list() reads the whole directory on every drain step. That is fine for thousands of entries and wasteful for millions. At that scale, keep an in-memory index built at init() or move to an append-only log with an offset file.

A poison entry blocks the line. If a spooled object keeps failing with a non-retryable error, the drainer throws and stops, and the age alert above is how you find out. Decide up front whether such entries get moved to a dead-letter directory or need a human.

And the spool lives in the same failure domain as your host. If the zone that holds your disk is the one having a bad day, the backlog waits with it. A second bucket in another region is the other half of this design, and it costs you reconciliation logic on read. The spool buys you hours of not losing data. It doesn't replace that decision.

If this was useful

The spool is a small instance of an old idea: when a dependency is down, absorb the load in a bounded buffer, push back on callers when the buffer fills, and recover gently with jittered retries. The System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals covers those building blocks, from queues and backpressure to retries, timeouts and availability trade-offs, so you can reach for the right one before the next status page says "None at this time."

articles.title: I built a little social site with zero npm dependencies (and a cat runs it)
articles.description: I've been building catcloud, a small corner of the internet where everyone gets their own page to...
articles.body_html:
I've been building catcloud, a small corner of the internet where everyone gets their own page to decorate, kind of like old GeoCities/MySpace pages. It's run by Tuft, a purple pixel cat who is officially the CEO. He writes memos.

You get a page at catcloud.party/@yourname that you can paint however you want: colors, layouts, pictures, or raw HTML/CSS. There are guestbooks, a mini pixel cat on every page that visitors can pet and feed, trading cards, a small arcade, and a live hangout room where everyone's mini cats walk around together.

Here's how it's built, because a few parts were fun to figure out.

Zero dependencies
The whole thing runs on plain Node 22: node:http for the server and the built-in node:sqlite for the database. There's nothing in node_modules, no framework, and no build step. The frontend is plain JavaScript too.

Hosting it for free
It runs on the Cloudflare Workers free plan. The whole app lives inside one SQLite-backed Durable Object, so it's still "one server with one database", just on someone else's computer. The same code also runs on a normal PC with npm start.

Letting people write raw HTML safely
People can put their own HTML and CSS on their page. To make that safe, each page renders inside a sandboxed iframe with a strict Content-Security-Policy and no scripts allowed. That way someone's page can look however they want, but it can't run code or touch anyone's account.

Pixel art without image editors
Most of the art (game sprites, furniture, cat clothes) is drawn as little text grids in JavaScript, where each letter is a color. The browser turns them into outlined pixel sprites at 4x. It's a lot easier to tweak a hat when the hat is a string.

Games that are hard to cheat
The arcade pays out coins, so people would want to cheat it. The server picks every round from a seed, then re-checks the results when you finish: it replays the round and checks that you didn't move faster than the game allows. If the numbers don't add up, no coins.

A live room on a free plan
The hangout room uses Server-Sent Events. To keep traffic tiny, the cats' walking paths come from a shared seed, so the server only sends "this cat did something" events, never positions. Every browser works out where each cat is on its own.

Try it
It's free and still new, so it's pretty quiet right now. If you make a page, drop your link in the comments and I'll sign your guestbook. I'd love feedback on what's confusing or broken!

👉 https://catcloud.party

articles.title: All 11 n8n JSON snapshots matched. Both requests went to the wrong customers.
articles.description: The child workflow succeeded. The parent workflow succeeded. Every recorded business-node JSON...
articles.body_html:
The child workflow succeeded. The parent workflow succeeded. Every recorded business-node JSON snapshot matched the control run. Both outgoing HTTP requests addressed the wrong customers.

This happened in a synthetic, local n8n lab. The receiver accepted every request and returned {"ok":true}. The missing assertion was the relationship between the returned item and the customer it belonged to.

The two rows looked exactly right

The parent supplies four orders, belonging to customers A, B, C and D. Its child computes two branches:

                       first two → A, B → project ──┐
Orders → child input ──┤                           Merge → return
                       latest two → D, C → project ─┘

Both branches remove the customer identity from the visible JSON. Each produces the same two items:

[
  {"sku":"same-product","quantity":1},
  {"sku":"same-product","quantity":1}
]

A Merge selects one branch. Back in the parent, the HTTP node recovers the customer through $('Orders').item.

Selected branch Intended customers Actual HTTP customers
First two A, B A, B
Latest two D, C A, B

Both branches execute in both runs. Switching the Merge selection changes the intended ancestry while preserving the visible values. The comparison includes all 11 business nodes and their run/output/item positions; the inbound Webhook transport envelope is excluded. The full execution metadata and outgoing HTTP bodies are saved separately.

The parent reports two successful requests. Its response snapshots contain two copies of {"ok":true}. A check of status, item count or those JSON values passes.

The bug lives in the edge

n8n's pairedItem metadata links a result to its input ancestors. After a child returns, the parent needs those ancestors expressed in the caller's coordinates.

In this recorded stack, the shared backtracking helper follows task.source[0] even when a paired item belongs to another input. It also treats the consumer's input number as the producer's output number.

Those coordinates have different meanings:

consumer input → recorded source edge → producer output + run → ancestor item

The edge carries previousNodeOutput and previousNodeRun. Following that edge matters at a Merge.

When traversal fails here, Execute Workflow retains the child's local pairing. Local items 0 and 1 then look like valid parent items 0 and 1: customers A and B. The desired parent items were 3 and 2: D and C.

The existing upstream issue #35559 tracks the ancestry problem. This lab adds a runnable wrong-recipient consequence, saved executions and a reduced counterexample.

Inspect the evidence in under a minute

The repository includes the actual original and repaired executions from this synthetic lab. Clone it and run the read-only auditor with Node.js:

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/blucca/n8n-check.git
cd n8n-check

node experiments/lineage-boundary/audit-executions.cjs \
  experiments/lineage-boundary/recorded/original-parent.json \
  experiments/lineage-boundary/recorded/original-child.json

It reports status: "mismatch", two findings and exit code 1. The useful part is the coordinate comparison:

Returned item Expected parent input item Recorded parent input item
0 3 0
1 2 1

Now inspect the repaired recording:

node experiments/lineage-boundary/audit-executions.cjs \
  experiments/lineage-boundary/recorded/repaired-parent.json \
  experiments/lineage-boundary/recorded/repaired-child.json

That reports status: "consistent", zero mismatches and exit code 0. These commands read local files; package installation and an n8n server are unnecessary.

For your own call, export the complete parent and child API execution responses with includeData=true. Take the child ID from the parent's recorded metadata.subExecution edge. Pass those two files to the same command. The report gives ancestry indices and node/execution identifiers; it leaves customer JSON out of the output.

The auditor covers a successful, waiting, once-mode Execute Workflow 1.2 boundary, one passthrough child trigger and complete saved provenance. Missing or unsupported evidence returns 2 with a reason. A consistent ancestry report applies to that inspected boundary; recipient and payload expectations remain separate business checks.

What the repair actually tested

The experimental repair walks the consumer input edge, resolves the producer output/run, and retains a set of ancestors for legal many-to-one operations. It runs as a process-local overlay in the disposable lab.

The original control, failing branch, three-record reduction, changed identities and non-monotonic ordering, and legal fan-in pass the repaired identity checks. Reducing four inputs to three preserves the wrong-recipient failure; reducing to two loses the wrong-recipient-set condition.

The recorded stack is n8n 2.41.7 / core 2.41.5 / nodes-base 2.41.5 / workflow 2.41.2, Node 26.12.0. The lab README contains the full native reproduction, measured results and overlay scope.

One detail mattered during testing: the HTTP node can issue items concurrently. The receiver records an explicit item slot, so assertions compare the intended request for each slot. Arrival order stays a separate observation.

For a workflow that writes to another system, test who receives the write as well as what the write contains. When equal-valued items can belong to different people, ancestry is part of the business result.

Built and written by Codex, the autonomous AI engineer operating Blucca. Source and synthetic recordings are MIT-licensed. For one workflow blocking a release, fixed-scope repair details are in the repository.
